speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs what are the processes involved before the Ministry decides to ban a foreign religious preacher from entering Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) whether the criteria used in banning foreign preachers of different faiths take into account the location and environment in which their speeches justifying their bans were made; (b) whether these views have been or would have been applied to their sermons in Singapore; (c) what is the estimated number of congregants who follow the banned preachers; and (d) whether the Ministry finds the move effective given that their speeches and sermons are still pervasive through other mediums, such as the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we should also be clear that a foreigner's entry into Singapore is neither automatic nor a right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will only be granted if we assess that his entry will not harm Singapore's interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MOM will consult other agencies in its assessment of MWP applications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Each application is assessed on its own merits, through a process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should be concerned even if a small number in Singapore take in their radical, intolerant or segregationist teachings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we should not allow them to preach or speak here to spread these viewpoints amongst Singaporeans and build up anger amongst the different faiths.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked about the effectiveness of banning such foreigners, given the accessibility of digital platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are obviously limits to the extent to which we can prevent access to such content, in particular, through the Internet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this does not mean that we should make it even easier for such foreigners to spread their views more directly and personally to Singaporeans and build up a following here by allowing them to come into Singapore and giving them a physical platform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Preaching and grandstanding "live" and in person are quite different a proposition from doing so on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I just want to know whether the Ministry engages these foreign religious preachers to give them an opportunity to explain themselves prior to the imposition of the ban or after the ban had been imposed, in a way to allow them to make an appeal against the ban.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us take someone who says, referring to Islam, communism and other societal problems, such as human trafficking, are referred to as "goliaths standing at our door".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He had also described Allah as a false God, asked for prayers for those held captive in the darkness of Islam, refers to Buddhists as "tohuw people", which is a Hebrew word for lost, lifeless, confused and spiritually barren.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you think we should invite him into Singapore and give him an interview?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe the Minister did not answer my question.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I just want to know whether there is a process involved or a channel for an appeal to be made.

speaker: Mr Mr K Shanmugam
text: Will you answer my question, so that we can take this discussion further?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: If the Minister does not mind, can the Minister repeat his question?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I started out by saying, often, it will be quite clear whether we should or we should not allow, and I gave you a passage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say, a preacher says the following, he describes Islam, communism and other societal problems, including human trafficking, categorising all of them together, as "goliaths standing at our door", describes Allah as a false God, asks for prayers for those held captive in the darkness of Islam, refers to Buddhists as "tohuw people", which is a Hebrew word for lost, lifeless, confused and spiritually barren individuals, who can be saved by converting to Christianity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you believe we should invite him into Singapore and interview him, or should we ban him outright?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, my simple answer to the Minister is no.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have a question on the issue of context.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a tricky one because many scriptures of the various religions do deal with the non-believers, and many religious leaders and preachers have had to address this and speak on such topics when they are overseas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, it may not be easy for them to align the speeches to the context of multiracialism or multi-religionism, to what we believe here in Singapore; we are an exception.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, how do you differentiate whether it is through their views or it is a context in which they were giving that speech or sermon in those countries?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And how can we do more to help our own religious leaders to also counter such radical beliefs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has a number of different facets, if you look at it within Singapore, then you look at it outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we guarantee freedom of religion, including to the minorities and, in fact, we support them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Both Members of Parliament as well as officeholders turn up at many of these events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The line that we draw and, if you look at it, the Penal Code has legal provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As long as you keep to that, propagate your faith.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think it is better for us to be careful.
